newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel 1996 budget deficit reaches 4.7 pct of GDP.
newsitem.headline: Israel 1996 budget deficit reaches 4.7 pct of GDP.

text.p: Israel's domestic budget deficit swelled to 4.7 percent of gross domestic product in 1996, nearly double its targeted level, the Finance Ministry said on Monday.

The deficit, excluding credit granted, came to a preliminary 14.4 billion shekels last year, compared with a planned 7.6 billion shekels. The Treasury had planned to hold the deficit to 2.5 percent of GDP.
The Treasury won spending cuts from this year in order to achieve a deficit target of 2.8 percent, including the domestic and foreign currency deficit.

"Initial analysis of the deficit's components shows that total government spending in 1996 was in accordance with plans; the big deviation in the size of the deficit resulted entirely from failing to meet revenue forecasts," the Treasury said.

In a separate report, the Treasury said tax revenues came to 95 billion shekels in 1996. This compared with 83.9 billion in 1995, or a real increase of 3.7 percent after adjusting changes in tax rates. However, it was below the projected 99.2 billion shekels.
Income and purchase taxes fell 0.5 percent from 1995 to 50.6 billion shekels while value-added tax and customs rose 4.1 percent to 42.2 billion shekels.
In December 1996 alone, the Israeli government posted a 4.4 billion deficit including credit granted, the Treasury said.
For full-year 1996, total spending was 124 billion shekels, not including debt service.

The deficit, including the foreign currency portion, was a smaller 11.4 billion shekels, or 3.7 percent of GDP, because of U.S. aid. The difference was especially pronounced last year because of the late payment of $1.2 billion in U.S. aid from 1995 during the 1996 year, the Treasury said.
Not accounting for this extra aid, the total deficit would have been 4.8 percent.

Last year's deficit was financed by raising a net 7.9 billion shekels in the local capital market, the equivalent of 3.5 billion shekels abroad and from 350 million shekels in revenues from privatisation.
Final figures will be published in a few months.
